books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the historical record; boundaries and dates from the Oregon boundary dispute. See Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 7, and 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 14.
stimulus.text:
| Proposal | Year | Boundary |
| United States claim | 1844–1846 | 54°40′ (the southern edge of Russian Alaska) |
| Offer made by the United States | 1845 | 49th parallel |
| British counter-proposal | 1845 | Columbia River |
| Oregon Treaty | June 15, 1846 | 49th parallel to the Strait of Georgia, then through the Strait of Juan de Fuca |

source: original; stimulus is a table compiled from the historical record of the Oregon boundary dispute
stem: The slogan “54°40′ or Fight” is best understood in light of the table as

options.text: a promise Polk made in his inaugural address to go to war with Britain.
options.misconception: The slogan was aimed at Polk, not spoken by him; Polk settled the dispute by treaty, not war.

options.text: the line Britain proposed as a compromise in 1845.
options.misconception: Britain proposed the Columbia River; 54°40′ was the American claim.

options.text: the boundary the Oregon Treaty finally established.
options.misconception: The treaty set the line at the 49th parallel, well south of 54°40′.

options.text: a demand for the fullest American claim, which the United States later gave up.

rationales.A: The slogan was directed at Polk by expansionists, not spoken by him, and Polk compromised rather than fighting Britain. Background: Princeton notes the slogan was aimed at Polk, not his own words.
rationales.B: Britain's counter-proposal was the Columbia River; 54°40′ was the American claim, not a British offer.
rationales.C: The treaty line was the 49th parallel, not 54°40′, so the slogan's line was not the settlement.
rationales.D: 54°40′ was the fullest American claim in the table, and the United States gave it up to settle at the 49th parallel.
rationales.general:
1. Find 54°40′ in the table. It is the United States' opening claim, the farthest north.
2. Find where the dispute ended. The treaty set the line at the 49th parallel, south of 54°40′.
3. Read the slogan against that gap. It demanded the full claim — and the full claim was the part given up.
Remember: a slogan can outlive the bargain. “54°40′ or Fight” sounds absolute, but the settlement was a compromise.
